opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think my view on this has evolved quite a bit. A couple of years ago, there was this strong narrative that every company would need dozens of bespoke models: one for legal, one for customer support, one for code, and so on. And I think what we've seen is that the general-purpose models have gotten so capable that, for a huge share of use cases, you don't need to train something from scratch. You get a lot of mileage out of a strong base model plus good retrieval, good tool use, and good prompting.

That said, I don't think specialization goes away. It shifts. Where I see it really mattering is when an organization has data and workflows that are genuinely unique to them, things that just aren't represented on the open web. Think about a bank's internal processes, a pharma company's proprietary research, or a manufacturer's operational data. In those settings, a general model is going to hit a ceiling, because it simply hasn't seen that kind of information. Customizing the model, whether that's fine-tuning or deeper post-training on their data, can make a meaningful difference in accuracy and reliability.

There's also a practical side: cost and latency. If you have a very high-volume, narrow task, you often don't want to run the biggest frontier model on every single request. A smaller, specialized model that's really good at that one thing can be far more efficient. And for a lot of enterprises, especially in regulated industries, there's the question of where the model runs and who controls it. Being able to deploy something tailored, privately, in their own environment, is a big deal.

So the way I'd frame it now is: start with a strong general model, connect it to your data and your tools, and see how far that gets you. Usually it gets you surprisingly far. Then specialize where the value is concentrated, where you have unique data, high volume, or strict requirements around performance and privacy. It's less "every team needs its own model" and more "be strategic about where customization actually moves the needle."

fable-5.1.text:
I think my view on that has shifted quite a lot over the last couple of years. If you'd asked me in 2023, I would have said that every enterprise is going to want its own fine-tuned model, trained on its own data, and that's going to be the dominant pattern. And there was a period where that was true, mostly because the base models weren't good enough. You had to specialize to get acceptable performance on a narrow task.

What's actually happened is that the general models have gotten so capable that a lot of the reasons you used to need a specialized model have just evaporated. The frontier model, with the right context, the right retrieval setup, the right tools plugged in, will outperform a model you fine-tuned eighteen months ago on your proprietary data. And it'll do it without you having to maintain a training pipeline, re-tune every time the base model updates, and deal with all the operational burden that comes with owning a model.

So I think the question has moved from "do I need my own model" to "how do I give a strong general model access to what's specific about my organization." And that's mostly a data and systems problem, not a modeling problem. It's about connecting the model to your documents, your databases, your internal tools, and doing that securely. That's where the real work is for most companies.

That said, I don't think specialization is dead. There are still real reasons to do it. Cost is one. If you're running something at enormous scale, a smaller model tuned for that task can be dramatically cheaper. Latency is another. And there are genuinely domain-specific cases, things like very specialized languages, highly regulated workflows, or tasks where the behavior you want is hard to express in a prompt, where fine-tuning or distillation still makes a lot of sense.

The framing I'd use now is: start with the general model, get it working with your data, and only specialize when you have a concrete reason, usually cost, latency, or a performance gap you can actually measure. Most organizations that start from the other direction end up building infrastructure they don't need.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful distinction is between having a model that’s capable of doing lots of things and having a system that’s really good at a particular job. You don’t necessarily need to train a separate model for every function in your organization. A lot of the specialization can come from giving the model the right context, connecting it to your internal information, and giving it the tools it needs to act.

But there are cases where a specialized model makes a lot of sense. If you’re doing the same task millions of times, you want something small, fast, and inexpensive that does that task reliably. You might use a more capable general model to help build that system, then deploy a smaller model for the actual workload.

So I’d start with the task and how you’re going to measure success. Does the model need knowledge it doesn’t have? Does it need to behave differently? Or is it already capable, but too expensive to run at the scale you need? Those are different problems, and they don’t all call for training another model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think specialization is going to be important, but that doesn’t necessarily mean every organization needs to train its own model from scratch. You can start with a really capable general model and then specialize it around the task, the data, and the constraints of the business.

There are a few reasons to do that. One is quality: a model that understands your terminology and your workflows can be much more useful. Another is efficiency. If you have a narrow task that you’re doing millions of times, you probably don’t want to use the biggest, most expensive model for every single request.

So I think you’ll see a mix within organizations: general models for the broad, open-ended work, and smaller, specialized models for particular processes. The important thing is to start with the problem you’re trying to solve and measure whether specialization actually improves the outcome.
